en: Carrying a thick dust of vermilion as if it were the blood spilling from the frontal globes of the elephants of Jambha’s enemies,
and appearing as if drenched by the streams of mineral-fluids from the slopes of the Sunrise Mountain,
may the dawn— red and equal in time to the radiance of a forest of lotuses— bring you prosperity.
May the ever-new rays of the sun, belonging to the solar orb, shine forth, illuminating the world.

Those rays which, desiring as it were to draw forth the Goddess of Fortune who is hidden within the hollows of the buds of the lotus-thicket for the sake of one prostrate in devotion, perform the opening of the lotus forest.
May those rays of the sun, possessing the luster of young sprouts— capable of destroying the terror of the world fallen into the darkness of the form of Time—
bring you auspiciousness as they fall equally upon the interiors of lotuses and upon the sharp peaks of mountains.

May the rays of the sun protect you— rays that remain identical at both the commencement and the conclusion of the day, proceeding without alternation across the courtyard of the palace of the three worlds,
and bearing intensely the heat born of continuous travel upon the path, as it were.
When the luster of the upper garment has faded away in the darkness, the sun, beholding the creatures whose veils have been removed,
spreads forth its rays like threads;
these rays, having suddenly become dense, [fill] the vast expanse of the ten directions as their state gradually becomes clear.
May they, constantly bestowing a stainless sky, grant you abundant auspiciousness. 4.

As if having first performed a welcoming reception for the Fire risen from the radiant mountain, they—by their very purity, as if out of grief for the medicinal herbs whose luster has been stolen by the Lord of Herbs (the Moon), now shorn of their light—put those herbs to shame.

May the dawn of the rays of the fierce-rayed sun, copper-red at morning as it strikes the eastern mountain— showing forth the rocks as if they were bleeding from wounds where their wings had been severed— be for your protection against undesired calamities.
(5) [They see] those with shattered noses, feet, and hands, with mangled limbs making gurgling and indistinct sounds.
May that Sun, whose unimpeded course is characterized by a double intensity of thick compassion for those long afflicted by the floods of sin, and who alone restores them to health;
may he, having been honored with offerings by the hosts of Siddhas, grant you prosperity.
May the rays of the Sun, who first assumed a dwarfed form and then likewise became tall, swiftly remove the obstruction from your feet. May they be compassionate toward you.
May the horses of the Sun, who traverse the expanse of the sky and thereafter fill the ten directions;
who, having torn away from the darkness like powerful enemies of the gods, swiftly pervade the universe;
and who, by their soaring playfulness, mock the lions—may they remove our hardships. 7.
May those [rays] grant [your desires]: they who, through their intense redness, greatly enhance the crimson nature of Aruṇa;
who possess the luster of blood from wounds caused by bits in the mouths of the chariot-horses as they toss their heads;
and who bestow the state of being mountain peaks upon the mountains, resting upon the summits of the lofty crags.
May those rays of the sun, which, swaying in the sky, have pierced the face of the day, bring you happiness.
Bestowing joy upon all creatures with waters drawn forth at the proper time and released in the forenoon, they scatter in every direction as the day declines and gather them back again;
they are like ships for crossing the ocean of worldly existence, which arises from long-standing suffering and is filled with fear, belonging to the Sun of radiant rays.
May the rays of light, the supreme among purifiers, produce for you boundless joy.

May they grant awakening— like a bed of vast lotus clusters— to those people who, with palms joined in salutation at the time of twilight, bow their heads in obeisance, for these rays are the sole cause for the destruction of bondage.
May those wish-fulfilling trees of yours—the expansion of your own minds—fulfill your vast aspirations; may they be like the rays of the sun, banners against the darkness of defilement. 10.
May they be like torrents, swift currents of wealth in times of distress, and may they instantly become a supporting hand for you on the precipice.

May the rays of the sun, which are like the sole lamps illuminating reality, acting as gatekeepers at the threshold of the bodies of yogis striving for liberation as they set out upon the very paths leading to the city of the Lord of the Thirty-three,
protect you from sin— those rays that bring happiness at the break of day. 11.
Moving eastward in the eastern quarter not long ago, they abandoned their status as beautiful crest-jewels upon the immovable mountain,
as if to pour forth abundant liquid yellow pigment for the high praise of the directions;
they were being honored by the steady eyes of the cakravāka birds with clever and affectionate cries.
May the rays of the fierce-rayed sun, acting as they are wont to do for those who have thought of them, bring about your final goal.
Those which are declared by the four-faced Brahmā to be the one light in the eyes, the two lights in the three worlds,
the five lights of living beings, and likewise the various six lights during the six seasons— may they [protect you].

May those seven hundred rays of the sun— which are praised by the thirty gods and the sages, which pervade the eight directions, and which attain their fullness at dawn— bestow auspiciousness upon you.
Having caused the entire universe to revolve and whirl, they appear as if exhausted and withered by their own heat.
May the rays of the sun—those which, like forest fires scorching the earth in summer, repeatedly drink its moisture;

which, as if afflicted by the excessive heat of their own drinking during the rainy season, vomit forth water; and which, in the winter, are no longer fierce—long bring about the destruction of your misfortunes.

At the dawn, when the luster of the lotus-eyes of the quarters was beginning to blossom, she appeared alone, having assumed a state exceedingly sweet to behold; her form was adorned with a slight tawny hue emerging from the first traces of full maturity.
May the thousand rays of the sun, like a row of beards, grant you protection.

May that emergence of the rays of the enemy of darkness, though slight, stand as sufficient protection for you— [the emergence] which was, as it were, praised by Kṛṣṇa, who feared the humiliation of his own body by the darkness, as if by the Creator who had settled comfortably within the hollow cave of a lotus just opened at dawn. 16.
Those who at dawn, having destroyed the darkness, cause the vast sky to expand, the ten long quarters to suddenly cast their boundaries into the waters of the oceans,
and the earth— with its expanse of mountains and cities— to appear broad once more;
by whom the lotus-beds are awakened and the world itself is brought back to life.
May the rays of you, who possess a thousandfold brilliance, swiftly cause that which is disagreeable to him to fall away.

May that rising of rays grant you auspiciousness— those rays which, as the sun of fierce brilliance wanders through the three worlds in dependence upon space and time, have attained a new name in the eastern quarter;
and which, as if out of compassion lest they wither like a lotus stalk so delicate, did not enter the realm of serpents.

May that mass of light, known as the Sun, protect you—he who shines not merely upon the side of the world-revealer (Lokāloka mountain), but for its very sake; he whose expansion is checked by the fear of shattering the upper shell of the cosmic egg, and whose limit in the expanse of heaven is defined solely by his own will. 19.
The dark night does not become one with the end of the world when darkness has vanished;
nor does the moon, the mountain-footed one, immediately meet its dissolution.
Indeed, there is no binding for those who offer palms joined in reverence, nor even for the grove of night-lotuses, when he rises.

May that light of the Lord of Day, which is to be beheld at dawn, grant you desires exceeding all [others]— that light which does not steal the luster of the lotuses but rather makes them more beautiful,
which does not possess the brilliance of the stars but utterly eclipses them, and which is ever-present.

May that singular light of the Sun, the destroyer of sins— which is unlike any ordinary eye and is the sole eye of the three worlds, incapable of being measured even by a moment or a day— be for your welfare.
As if out of a thirst for the touch of water cooler than the dew-drops of night, she quickly abandoned the earth;
as if to awaken the lotuses from the trunks of the elephants of the quarters, she swiftly overspread the regions of space;
and at dawn, as if out of compassion, she traversed even the station of Viṣṇu with extreme speed to reach the farthest distance.

May the unrestrained, radiant splendor of the Sun burn away your ill omens. May that light—which is unattainable even for the mountain that is being shattered by the fierce force of the winds at the end of the eon;
which possesses an intensely emitted, brilliant beauty by day; and which is never abandoned by the collyrium of darkness—protect you.
May that very flame of the lamp which lights all the continents—having attained its birth from the sun and never again returning to extinction—though appearing in another form, grant you joy;
May the radiant splendor of the Sun—she who is ever lofty even during the onset of dawn and the disturbances of the day’s passing;
she who is utterly incapable of dwelling for even a moment in the company of darkness—be like a pleasing light for you, so that you may attain the desired object. 24.
Bearing a spear that swiftly quelled the heavy arrogance of Tāraka’s strength, effortlessly casting even the fire-god Śikhin down while shining with the luster of a brilliant moonstone,
it would bring an exceeding delight to the eyes even in the midst of darkness.
May the child [Kārttikeya], who—like another Guha—is like the heat of the sun to the lotus, yet like Guha to the goddess Lakṣmī;
May the splendor of the sun— the red glow of the twilight,
which at the time of dawn unrolls the entire world like a painting—
bring you incomparable joy to the eyes, like a brush for the sharp-rayed one.
Is this a path from Mount Sumeru coming here, reddened by the pollen of ruby-lotuses;
or is it the Vaijayantī banner of his chariot, fashioned with saffron-dyed cloth; or is it a row of crimson chowries on the heads of the horses at the front, shaken by the world?
May the radiance of the sun, the dispeller of darkness, which is gazed upon with apprehension, be for your protection at dawn.

That light which, though it destroys the gloom, does not yet scorch; which possesses luster, yet does not reveal its full form; and which, even after withdrawing its brilliance during the night, does not bestow the splendor of day to a greater degree—may that radiance be yours.
May he not cease at dawn, fulfilling your hopes with his form complete; for the light of the sun has begun its youthful descent into the expanse of the sky of hope.
(28) That which is the cause of intense Nirvana, though vast, yet exceedingly subtle.

May that twofold light of the sun—the external and the internal—protect you: that which is perceptible and that which is beyond perception, that which is perishable and that which is eternal here, and that which is well-known to all in the world yet known by only a few yogins. 29
That which serves to adorn jewels, having found its place by virtue of a fixed location; that which enables fire to burn wood and the like through its own inherent dullness;
and that which brings joy to the moon—may that very principle, which is the ornament of the three worlds, the burner of evil, and delightful with its rain, swiftly [attain] you.
Because it produces a greater effect through its abundance, the single solar radiance alone [overcomes all others]. 30.
With eyes closing, ears dulled, tongue inert, the function of the nose suppressed, the skin incapable of its own activity, the mind stolen away, and nothing remaining but mere breath;
May the ancient splendor of the Sun, who— like a medicine that raises the world bitten by the serpent of Time— having fallen with drooping limbs, removes your misfortune from its position;
he who forcibly dispels the entirety of the nocturnal waters, which resemble a few drops of tears.
With its crimson luster gradually diminished and its lingering defects long since dispelled,
may the ancient course of the sun’s rays— the other form of the perfected collyrium— swiftly grant you a clear vision of the Eye of the Three Worlds, while destroying all that is hostile to you.
Having become the source of the onset of defeat for Jambha, the shatterer of mountains, at the eastern quarter of the bright-rayed sun;
assuming a tawny hue, bold as the blooming of a fresh lotus;
the radiance of the sun, most beautiful, was the first ornament of this palace of the three worlds.
May that radiant splendor, which dispels delusion, shine forth for the sake of your manifestation of power—
she who was embraced by the Night, like a maiden eager for a new garden of the world, with nectar poured from the jar of the moon.
May the light of the sun bring you joy— rising from the basin-like horizon of the eastern mountain, like the first sprout of the tree of day, possessing a luster resembling young coral shoots; which,
in some places, is split by the radiance of fresh corals as if by the glow of a newly risen dawn.

May the Sun-like Splendor—whose interior is formidable with a mass of light from the jewels of his skin, limbs, and stars; who, in some places, drinks up the heap of darkness like the ocean that possesses the entirety of black beauty within; and who is like the primordial submarine fire (Aurva) yet unprecedented—stand for the burning away of your sins.

He who, having shattered [the darkness], is praised by the Gandharvas with words charming from the intermingling of prose and verse, and by the ancient sages such as Nārada and others who know the Vedas, with the playing of musical instruments;
and he, rising instantly, attains the youth of the world once again.
May this Uddyota, who has illuminated the sky and outshone the sun, dispel your faults today—

[faults] which have been diminished by the flow of moonstones, whose darkness has vanished due to the appearance of the stars, and which have perished through the disappearance of the light of the medicinal herbs whose brilliance was eclipsed by the moon. 36.1–2.

May that morning radiance of the moon protect you—the moon which, having vanished behind the edge of the eastern slope, is now visible from afar for a moment; yet it does not protect as much while it is still fully manifest.
On the mountain peak at sunrise, she [the dawn] shines, while the forests are regaining their youth with petals reddened by the rising sun.

May that row of lotus pollen grant the pacification of worldly existence— pollen which is beautiful, previously enjoyed by bees, avoiding the low-lying edges of the hollows, exceedingly slender, and possessing a luster equal to the radiance of the sun— as it rises simultaneously with its companion. 38.
She who brings forth the beauty of blossoming lotuses for the sake of the waters, not for their heat; who, when beheld, bestows mere light upon the eyes but never inflicts injury;
she who first rises from the eastern mountain and thereafter purifies the face of the quarters of the sky.
May that ancient goddess, the sole abode of the path of praise, drive away your sins— she who shines forth,
whose eloquence is fit to be the teacher even of Vācaspati (Bṛhaspati) and of the four faces of Brahmā, which are skilled in the elaborations of the Vedas and have uttered the four Ṛks.
May that Fire-god, whose pure conduct cannot be faulted even when scrutinized intensely in his various forms, and whose ancient splendor shines forth brightly, long increase your prosperity.
On his head is the red mineral of the mountain, on the trees are sprouts, and in the ocean is a mass of coral. 40.
May that radiance of the sun at dawn, which arises from the thick vermilion dust freshly placed upon the heads of the lordly elephants of the quarters,
and which constitutes a portion of the splendor at the boundary between the sky and the golden peaks of the divine mountains, grant you well-being through its crimson glow. 41.
When the moon— the Kālakūṭa poison of darkness— has been swallowed by the head of the mountain of the setting sun,
and the morning Pārijāta tree has manifested before us with its sprouts of dawn-red,
the rising goddess of the day is gazed upon by the sharp-rayed sun, who is himself made clearer by his bright yellow and reddish garments.
May Lakṣmī, like Lakṣmī herself, resting upon the cupped palms of her hands which resemble blossoming lotuses, be for your welfare.
Neither the ocean was her birthplace, nor were the Kaustubha jewel and other gems her kinsmen born from her womb;
neither the lotus was in her hand, nor was the chest of the enemy of Naraka her dwelling place.
She is like another embodiment of splendor, establishing her own unique order throughout the three worlds.
May that Śrī, who has emerged from the orb of the cool-rayed moon, bestow blessings upon you.
May those horses protect the worlds— horses who, leaping up with great agility over the unbroken surface of golden stones, have surpassed the speed of the wind by their swiftness;
and on Mount Meru, whose path they traverse even without the rising of other signs, the sun’s steeds proclaim their course.
The sacrificial fire upon the jeweled stone altars of the sun-gem, blazing with intense radiance as it rises,

scorches their backs with its rays; due to being so close, these rays inflict excessive burning, and they suffer from exhaustion as they dry up through heavy panting, which is as broad as the entire path of the three heavens traversed in a single day.
May the horses of the Sun, whose necks are straightened by the spray from the nearby celestial Gaṅgā and whose foreheads are bowed down, hasten for the destruction of your enemies with intense speed.
Thinking them to be other horses at their side, they gallop along, their bodies visible against the crystal slabs of the mountain slopes.

May the row of the sun’s horses protect you—horses whose forms are visible through their resemblance to ruby stones on the slopes of Mount Meru as they pass over them on the eighth day of the waning moon, yet whose bodies appear obscured by the emerald girdle of the mountain;
horses whose movement is steady as they gain their turn at the summit, though their reins are strained. 46.

Carrying her playful waves as she was drawn far away from the celestial river by the forceful command of the Subduer of Poison (Viṣṇu), she surpassed the speed of his chariot with her own velocity; thus,
as her own green expanse was extended without artifice, she displayed the beauty of her abundant foam.
May the row of horses, like another Yamunā river of heat, pacify your misfortunes.
At the edge of the path on Mount Sumeru, seeing the hosts of celestial beings bowing down, the faces of the kinnarīs are bent with shame as they hide their mouths behind their backs.
May the neighing of the horses of the Uneven-Haired One (Viṣṇu)— which produces a slight, slow gait as they move with their throbbing necks half-turned—
simultaneously cast away your sins.
Shaking off masses of clouds on both sides, those steeds are like wings, green with their own luster.
May the horses of the Sun, as they travel through the sky as if flying by the force of their gait— brilliant-faced with bits raised against their palates and dripping with blood—
acting like parrots upon the rows of branches at the tops of the heart-pleasing trees on the peaks of the Golden Mountain, grant you prosperity.
Thus ends the description of the horse:
on the stage of the mountain peak at dawn, the beauty of which was visible as the curtain of night was withdrawn, the moon—
acting as the stage director— scattered the handful of unprecedented flowers that were the clusters of stars.

May the son of the Sun (Aruna) protect you, he who, having established his footing upon those four quarters that possess radiance like the four watches of the day, introduces for you the great drama of the world’s wandering;

Wandering through the world with partiality due to his own inclination, yet possessing equal regard for all, the sole witness of every action, and the enemy of the eyes and ears— he who is a treasury of power and splendors, though equal in seniority of age, may that thighless one (Viṣṇu) be your destroyer of sin, ever new in his majesty.

May that charioteer of the thousand-rayed sun grant you abundant protection— he who was gazed upon with humility in the sky by throngs of Siddhas bowing from afar after they had offered him the respectful water-offering (argha),
as he drank at dawn the very light of the moon which flows like a continuous stream of cold nectar.
He who, like a fire that has been kindled at first from wood and the like, blazes intensely at the beginning but later serves the sun [only feebly].

He who, at the beginning of the day and at the time of its departure, releases his rays and withdraws them again; who is independent, whose power is renowned like that of a goad, and who is constantly intent upon treading upon the feet of Hari;
he who, through the excellence of Time, forcibly imposes lightness upon the twice-born lords.
May that Aruṇa protect you—he whom Pūṣan, pleased by his service, made as if equal to himself while saving him.
Like an axe for the dark vine of night, like a flame for the forest-fire of darkness,
like the eastern quarter raised aloft at dawn to seize the grove of moon-lotuses,
it was the forefinger that broke the unity of heaven and earth, like a boundary-mark and like the creator of universal awakening.
May the trainer of your mounts remove the misfortune of the Lord of Wealth.

Like the east wind from the rising cloud, like smoke from a falling fire, like the primordial creation of the universe, and like the *praṇava* which purifies the entire mass of the Vedas—may he do so. (54)

May the son of Vinatā, who is like the joyful proclamation of Nandin to the enemy of Madana (Śiva) desiring the festival of the twilight dance, bestow happiness upon you as he stands before the chariot of Sūrya, his shoulders firmly resting upon the surface of its arm-guard made of refined gold. 55.
May he whose shoulders are embraced by the slopes of arm-guards of molten gold [grant you well-being].

May that preceptor of the enemy of Kadraveya’s sons— the emerald that, seated upon the chariot-horses, shines like a ruby and seems to bestow a magnificent ornament upon Meru, the lord of the mountain ranges— swiftly drive your sins far away. 56
Having brought the horses under control as if they were seven enclosures with a whip resembling a cane,
and having swiftly cast the mass of darkness far away like other people,
may he who was formerly at the front of the chariot protect you, pointing out the lords of the earth.

O Vajrin, you were formerly the gatekeeper for the Lord of Day (the Sun) when he was intent on bestowing his station upon the three worlds; O Agni, you shine with your lotus-thicket of eyes blossomed;
O Yama, having bowed to our father, lead [him] away from the side of the horse.
"O Rākṣasas, you have been seen; O Mahiṣa, you are watched! O Pracetas, sprinkle the horses; O Pavana, possess speed!
O Vittapa, you are known!"—speaking thus, "I bow to Śarva," may he protect the presiding deities in every direction.
"O Pūṣan, you are our leader;
do not seize us with the nooses of Varuṇa, the guardian of the quarters and the ruddy one. Abandon craving for the sake of grasping; indeed, my chariot does not travel with but a single wheel."

May he protect you—he whom the Sun instructs, saying: "Why do you desire Uccaiḥśravas, the eighth horse of the enemy of Vṛtra, when you are merely a vehicle? You have abandoned all other considerations; your sole purpose is the welfare of the universe.
He whose desires are severed by the absence of delusion, whose body is never overcome by fatigue, and who is not even parched of mouth.
May that Sun, the leader of the luminaries, consume for you all things other than the path— He who, having pervaded the three worlds, traverses them with his most intense rays,
while his row of horses, dark as emeralds, appears from afar like a line of clouds on the horizon.
Sinking with their dull hooves and maces submerged within the sands of the celestial river, leaping over the series of caves, stumbling upon the mountain ranges of the Golden Peak,
and having traveled far across the plains of *dūrvā* grass, they have not yet come to rest upon the emerald floor.

May the chariot of the Sun, descending through the path of the sky at midday, bestow prosperity upon you— the chariot which is driven by tawny steeds with long limbs, whose wheels turn without friction or sound, whose horses stretch their necks upward while their heads bow in a forced and contrary salutation.

May he who, by his occupying the position of incomparable greatness, was formerly brought to that state by Aryaman— who, skilled in the ritual for destroying the mass of darkness, bore a thousand rays—
now [protects] those who are utterly exhausted and unable to bear their burden, as if it were the weight of the winds.
May the chariot of the Sun be for your victory over evil as it moves from one aggregate to another;
it bears venomous serpents before it as if to swallow the yoke-pins that have become its traces,
and it possesses the beauty of a vast flapping of wings formed by rows of clouds spread out in two directions.

May that chariot of Savitṛ, whose path is subject to the will of Hari, carry you swiftly like Garuḍa— its rear-guard delighted by its unsurpassed speed, casting aside all sin. It is the lightest of things, traversing in a single day the long path of the three worlds.

May that very chariot of the Sun protect you—whose movement is so difficult to perceive; which, upon the back of Mount Meru, grinds the heads of those with the luster of crushed gems and stones; and which stands above all things, yet again appears as if below the summit of that mountain.

May there be well-being from those [chariots] whose foremost poles are held aloft, whose moon-like banners flutter in the wind, which repeatedly inflict pain upon the wheel when Rāhu approaches them from afar with a desire to swallow them,
and whose waters are the spray from the celestial river shaken by the effortless sighs of weary horses.
Desirous of giving the entire world to the Lord of Heaven,
they fastened protection to the axle with amulet-bracelets, joined the tips of the yoke to the pole,
offered incense at the hitching-post, and cast flowers within the range of the chariot’s pole.

May that Sun, whose chariot is drawn by horses, dispel your misfortunes— he whom the wives of the Siddhas, moving along the celestial path at the three junctions of the day, worship with sandalwood water as they converse.
His flanks are constantly struck on both sides by the swift hooves of his horses, which scatter clouds of golden dust.

May the single-track chariot-path of the Sun, its rim sinking under the weight of the unceasingly revolving wheel, shatter the cloud atop the summit of Mount Meru— like the celestial river (Ganges) made grey by the sandbanks revealed when its waters are dried up by the sun's own heat. 68.
The path followed incessantly by those who do not delay in bowing down is indeed a trail of dust;
it is the powder of the host of stars ground by the wheel spinning with fierce speed.
The neighing of the steeds and the roar of the rim fill the caves of the divine mountain peaks.
May that chariot of the fiercely radiant one protect you—[a chariot] whose distinct marks are manifest both in heaven and on earth.

May we not find ourselves unable to pay homage to the hosts of the most excellent gods, who, though their celestial chariots are motionless as they spread across the heavens, carry an intense surge of joy while dwelling upon the Mandara mountain— which resembles a palace, is soft, and possesses abundant sandy banks within the Mandākinī river.
May the chariot of the Sun-god, adorned with *mandāra* flowers and bearing the enemy of the lotus (*ari*), be for your delight!
May the Discus-bearer [Viṣṇu] protect the row of wheel-spokes; Hari likewise the horses; Dhūrjaṭi [Śiva] the ends of the banners on the pole;
the Lord of Stars [the Moon] the axle; Varuṇa the Aruṇa [the charioteer]; and Kubera the tip of the pole.
May that chariot of the sun—the impetus of the gods, which belongs to him who is eternally intent upon benefiting the world—protect you;
it is praised daily by the Siddhas and Sādhyas with Maruts, who, though eyeless, have prepared their equipment at its base with hearts gladdened by joy. 71.
May that chariot of the cool-rayed moon, which was praised at the feet of Viṣṇu as he swiftly dragged it with force,
and which now wanders incessantly through the ocean of the sky like a second Mount Mandara of incomparable majesty, bestow upon you boundless prosperity. 72.
Thus ends the description of the chariot:
that which is the superior seed of days, the collyrium for the eyes that removes darkness,
the gateway for those partaking in liberation, and the sole abode of all the lights of the universe.

May that great orb of the Lord of the Quarters— whose rain is a reservoir of water, whose earth is a vessel for drinking the nectar of essence, and which is complete with the radiance of the sun— bestow upon you perfect auspiciousness.
It is like the ocean’s water swelling at the shore, and like the sky when the foremost planets and stars have half-risen.
May the orb of the sun, appearing like the face of Spring with its first blossoming buds slightly revealed,
which has become the crest-ornament upon the eastern mountain— dispelling the densest darkness with its emerging rays— pacify your misfortunes this morning. (74)
By him [the mountain], who is like a mountain of blazing, molten gold inlaid with rubies,
which is the superior mass of filaments for the blue lotus of the swarm of bees;
and which is the most honored sign upon the head of the serpent of Time, a great jewel indeed!
May that orb of the radiant-rayed sun, the flawless ornament of the world, protect you in the morning.
Who is the protector of the stars? The moon falls like a drop of dew;
on the chest of the enemy of Smara (Śiva), his eye has faded, and the Kaustubha gem of the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) no longer shines.
May that orb of the Sun, rising there where its radiance seems as if eclipsed by fire, purify you— stealing away the darkness both in heaven and on earth with its great splendors.
It shines forth first in the east and from which it rises, it is therefore called "Prācya" (the Eastern).
May that solar orb of the Sun— which is radiant at midday, by whose light the day is produced,
which sustains the worlds in turn, which is the life-force of all beings, which bestows grace upon the universe, and which creates the entire world— be for your liberation. 77
By that [heat] of the moon’s rays, the abodes of sea-monsters—imitating the parched state of the sandy shores of the Love-god’s lutes—dry up;
and the mountains, heated and bursting asunder, flash like sparks at the end of an eon, resembling sesame seeds.
Out of fear that this might suddenly consume the three worlds, the sun with difficulty maintains its own radiance.
May that mandala of yours bring joy, which, having withdrawn its mere radiance, creates a subtle light;
it has burst forth from the lake of the rising garden, tearing asunder the thick mire of dense darkness, with its sides of petals shimmering with an unceasing, reddish glow.
May that great orb of the fierce-rayed sun bring you auspiciousness— like a lotus—
which is repeatedly surrounded by Rāhu, who takes the form of a swarm of bees for the sake of satisfaction;
and which, though it does not burn the eyes of the enemy of Dakṣa, fulfills every desire before them.

May that orb of the Sun protect you—honored by the Maruts, which serves as the vessel for those who practice self-restraint in the ocean of worldly existence; which, though wandering eternally through the universe without weariness, destroys the delusion of all beings; and which, performing seemingly contradictory actions, is yet the bestower of welfare.
Thus ends the description of the mandala,
which was recited repeatedly by the Siddhas with their established conclusions, by the wise who followed the prescribed rites with flattering words,
by the chief Gandharvas with song, and by the lords of serpents and the Yātudhānas with self-restraint.

May the Sun—whose rising is worshipped by the entire universe, whose praises are commenced at dawn with great devotion by the lords of sages and those seeking liberation who are exceedingly joyful in mind—protect you.
[He is so called] because of his proximity to light and because of the heat of the horizon which is most intensely radiant. 81.

May the Sun protect you as he wanders all around the Mountain of Gold, acting like one intent on its examination through three modes: by means of the unhesitating blows from the hoof-prints of horses galloping unhindered over the slopes; by the friction caused by the revolving parts of chariots moving without obstruction; and by his own heat.
The dry [trees] were not scorched by the celestial river with its blossoming golden lotuses; nor was the splendor of the Nandana grove utterly consumed so as to become unfit for enjoyment.
Nor did the peaks of the mountain of the immortals—their surfaces polished like silver—melt away swiftly.
May that Sun, whose blazing splendor softens even the path of the heavens through his compassion, protect you.

He is not merely the cause for the end of darkness; he also brings about the awakening of the lotuses at his very feet, and not only that, but he also effects the purification of the sin of those who possess a single-minded devotion to him.
May Aryaman—the creator of even the highest goods, and not merely of days; he who, with a single effort and desire, has accomplished the vast work of the universe—protect you.
[He is he] whose body has become utterly exhausted, having abandoned all movement and resorted to the surface of his bed.
May that Sun protect you—he by whose setting the world of living beings becomes filled with doubt regarding its very existence, suddenly beholding the ten directions as darkness;
exhausted by sighs and distress, the living world becomes utterly dependent on another, as if overcome by grief, when he has departed without causing the rising of other suns. 85.
Though fickle, he traverses the worlds; yet, when intent on performing service for them, he resorts to the pinnacle of steadfastness.
Though he makes the vision of men crooked, he renders their inner being exceedingly auspicious. He who is the cause even of asceticism for the self-restrained, bestows the singular liberation.
May that Sun, who brings about a transformation even greater than his previous state, be for your prosperity.

(86) The time of the season does not fail its fruit; rain does not fail the medicinal herbs; the gods are not satisfied with what is undesired; the wind does not carry away the stars of stainless luster.
The quarters of the sky remain peaceful and do not overstep their bounds; the oceans hold their limits, and the mountains bear the earth.
May that Sun, by whom the three worlds thus do not waver and yet shine, stand for your prosperity. 87
On Kailāsa, the one clad in animal skins (Śiva) sports, his body weary from the fear of separation;
Padmanābha (Viṣṇu), exhausted, sleeps upon the great serpent-bed in the ocean without disguise;
and Svayambhū (Brahmā), intent solely on the practice of yoga, passes his entire day.
May that Sun, who bears the heavy burden of thought for the three worlds and who is the sovereign of the universe, protect you all.
That which is this maṇḍala shining in the sky is the sun; those rays of his that shine are the Ṛg-verses, and those [spots] that gleam are the Sāman-chants.
This person within the maṇḍala, though minute, is the Yajus-formulas.
Thus, he who knows him as consisting of the three Vedas is himself the complete knower of the Vedas and the altar of knowledge.
May that Sun, the primordial source of both heaven and liberation, himself uncreated, be for your prosperity. May he,
along with all the gods led by Vāsava, whose splendor is as sharp as the enemy of the inhabitants of heaven,
protect this world well, even though they are all equally sons of Aditi.

May that Sun, by whom the name "Āditya" was bestowed upon himself through his unsurpassed qualities, and who is praised by the throngs of gods and sages worshipped by the three worlds, grant you prosperity.
By the rain from his abode, he makes the earth on this world composed of water and purifying even when merely remembered;
by the power of his fire, he repeatedly performs sacrifice with desired objects even when withdrawn into the sky,
fashioned from the moon during the dark fortnight.
Thus may the Sun, bearing his own form like Bhava [Śiva], protect you from the eightfold worldly existence—
his foot-beauty made manifest by the fragrance of the lotus-beds awakened at dawn,
and being carried through the sky with devotion by the son of Vinatā, who has abandoned the great torment of rising [from the ocean].

May that Sun-god, the Lord of days, protect you—He who, like another Murāri (Viṣṇu), is praised by the gods, and who, surpassing all other worlds, has reached the western horizon with His seven horses; May that source of rays be for your immediate success—he who stands above the three worlds with a supreme and insurmountable splendor; whose face, with its four quarters, is auspicious and bright with a serene luster; who is divided into two parts like the Creator, yet manifests the beauty of a lotus. 93.

May he whose twelve-fold self was revealed at the end of the age of inauspiciousness— the Sun, who shows the ten directions including the mountains, the earth, the rivers, and the intermediate points, and whose likeness is never seen by those with hundreds of eyes even in the realm of the Thirty-three Gods— grant you prosperity.
May he who, through his extraordinary power, instructs the horses and devours the venomous serpents by the mere knowledge of their intentions—[may he protect us].
For him, the sacred bathing places of lakes, rivers, ponds, waterfalls, and lotus-beds have become useless. 94.
The waters of the ocean do not dispel the terrifying and inauspicious danger that follows from falling into abysses;
nor do the waters of the celestial river, though they remove impurity, save those who sink therein.
May he, the sole cause of the day, grant you welfare—he who went to rescue other worlds. 95

This [universe] was as if submerged in the mud of the netherworld, enveloped in dense darkness alone; it was unknown, inconceivable, devoid of perception, and characterized by such a state within, as if asleep—
exactly as it becomes at night after every creation.
May that Sun, by whose separation the three worlds [suffer], protect you—he whose rising is equal to his setting.
For that which is the western mountain on this continent is indeed the eastern mountain elsewhere;
that which is night here with the brilliance of the shining moon is a day of intense heat elsewhere.

May that Lord of Days, the cause of the welfare of the world through His own sovereign power, protect you— He who, by His authority, ordains both place and time, yet is not limited by whatever place or time He may choose to guard.
(97) May He protect us from those fierce and exalted [demons], whose heavy burden consists of the voracious devouring of the foremost planets and the moon, and who are not yet fully assembled.
Rising over the mountain of sunrise, making the earth appear white with his fresh and slightly fierce rays like a herd of cattle,

may that leader of the planets bestow welfare upon you at the beginning of the days— he who, with his intense brilliance, seems to melt the very stones of the celestial city atop the mountain peaks, and may he dry up the dense darkness. 98.
The source of the Sāman chants is Vidhātṛ; Madhupuru is Ajita; Dhūrjaṭi is Śaṅkara;
he is Mṛtyu, Kāla, the Lord of Alakā who is Dhanada, and Pāvaka who is Jātavedas.
Thus, the names of the nectar-eaters (the gods) have arisen by chance, like the word "ḍavittha" and others.
May that Sun, who is the one denoted by all these [names] through his corresponding qualities, protect you!

Thus it is concluded: May he who is like no other, who at all times and in every way bestows benefit upon the worlds in every possible manner—that thousand-rayed one (the Sun)—grant you that which is prayed for.
One hundred verses were composed with devotion by the illustrious Mayūra for the prosperity of the world.
And that man who, being disciplined, should recite these even once, becomes liberated from all sins;
by the grace of the Sun, he obtains here health, excellent poetic skill, intellect, incomparable strength, beauty, longevity, knowledge, sovereignty, wealth, and even a son. 101
